claims.text: The reference material is a refractory high-entropy alloy in a predominantly disordered, solution-treated or as-cast condition with minimal preexisting nanoprecipitates.
A sub-transus aging treatment for a controlled time can induce nucleation and growth of B2-ordered precipitates in the refractory HEA.
Appropriate aging parameters will produce a uniform dispersion of B2 precipitates with sizes on the order of tens of nanometers.
The nanoscale B2 precipitates will retain coherent interfaces with the matrix.
Coherent nanoscale B2 precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Dislocation obstruction by the precipitates produces precipitation hardening and raises yield strength.
Coherent precipitate interfaces and an optimal precipitate volume fraction promote progressive, multistage strain hardening.
Progressive multistage strain hardening delays localized plastic instability and thereby sustains ductility.
Coherent precipitate interfaces can avoid a marked decrease in ductility.
Relative to the unaged baseline, the aged refractory HEA will gain several hundred MPa in yield strength.
The yield-strength increase will occur with only a modest loss of ductility or with ductility preserved.
The aged alloy will therefore have a superior strength–plasticity combination to the solution-treated or as-cast baseline.
The beneficial response requires precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction to remain within an optimal range.
Overaging that causes B2 coarsening or an excessive B2 volume fraction can compromise ductility and embrittle the alloy.
The proposed interaction mechanism applies at ambient testing temperature but may differ at very high or cryogenic temperatures.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing identically composed aged and solution-treated samples using microscopy, diffraction, and room-temperature tensile testing.
